Testers occupied its offices and that customer meetings have had to be relocated or cancelled.

In the past week, it's held public meetings to discuss its arguments and on Saturday, the IFA plans to protest outside the Agriculture Minister's constituency office in Newbridge.

Ireland's national energy grid faces three tough winters ahead with demand for electricity forecast to outstrip normal levels of supply.
That's according to an assessment published this morning by the operator Airgrid.
It says peak electricity demand will rise by 19% by 2035, driven by data centres, technology companies, electric vehicles and a move to heat pumps.
And new supply is not arriving fast enough to keep up with demand.

Nobody from Airgrid was available to talk us through their report this morning, but we are pleased to be joined by Professor Breno Gallicor, Director of the Murray Institute and Associate Vice President of Sustainability at University College Cork.
Good morning and welcome to the programme.
Good morning.
We know that demand for electricity is growing for the reasons I've just set out there and new capacity isn't coming fast enough.
What does all of that mean then for households and for businesses over the next few years?
Well, it means we've work to do and it raises a number of concerns.
And I must say this report is both very welcome and very timely in terms of flagging these issues.
Airgrid produce this report each year.
It provides a kind of 10-year horizon, a look ahead.
That's what...
What is expected in terms of the growth in demand for electricity?
What is the expectation in terms of the delivery of additional or changes in supply?
Because the changes in supply are not always about additional growth.
I mean, we have successfully and correctly phased out peat use for electricity generation.
We phased out coal use for electricity generation.
All over the space in the last five years.
And then once they've assessed the trends in terms of demand and supply, they ask that important question of will we have enough power in our electricity system to meet our needs?
Yes.
And over the next two years, we're finding that the system, that the electricity grid is going to be under a lot of pressure.
We know that the report says that by 2030, 32% of all electricity demand is expected to come from data centres and new technology loads.
That seems like an enormous amount of capacity being used by just one sector.
I mean, is it viable to continue growing the technology and data centre sectors when the grid is under so much pressure?

So at the moment, it's already about 22% of our electricity is coming from data centres.
And that would be greater, for example, than the amount used by rural homes.
So it is a very significant increase in electricity.
Demand.
And there's two challenges associated with that.
Well, there's probably more than two, but two that jump to mind are the need to accelerate supply, but also the need to make sure we do that and at the same time continue our journey.
of phasing out fossil fuels.
Because we've seen what the reliance on natural gas has done to our electricity bills over the last number of years.

So it's a real challenge, but that's why it's welcome and timely, because then it points to the need for policy solutions to accelerate the supply of electricity, particularly wind energy, solar energy batteries.
We do have a third, another interconnector on the way, the Celtic interconnector, which gives us a bit of a...
Respite in the period 2028 to the early 2030s.
But we really need to, I mean, what it points out to me is that we need to accelerate the supply of electricity from wind, solar and batteries.
And also we need to, you know, really do some more careful analysis, more detailed analysis on the...
The data centre growth, what will that mean in terms of, you know, can we sufficiently meet our electricity demands?
What does that mean for electricity prices?
And what does that mean for the transition away from fossil fuels?
Yes, but because while the policy is to not to stop the growth of data centres, there's also a policy and a plan to build 300,000 new homes between now and 2030.

when the grid is under so much pressure at the moment.
Well, this is the question.
This is an open question.
And this is why I think the analysis is very timely, because it means we need to look at really more closely at these different kind of and sometimes.
Conflicting policy requirements in terms of the need for additional homes, which is very clear to us all.
The need for data centres in terms of what are the costs and benefits associated with that.
And our ability to accelerate and we really need to drive that acceleration of the growth of electricity supply.
Yes.
All those three things in tandem.
And there have been long delays in driving that growth.
What additional capacity then can be turned on for the periods, especially in the next two to three winters, when we're going to need more power?
What capacity is there?
Well, we do have a lot of wind farms and solar energy and batteries in the pipeline, you know, in terms of applications in for grid connection agreements and for planning permission.
I mean, one of the challenges is, for example, we don't have enough planners.
So there's timelines that could be accelerated in terms of planning decisions around wind farms, solar farms and batteries.
But they're clogged up in the system at the moment.
So that's something that could be rectified.
But again, it's a policy decision that would require that investment.
But that's just one small example of what can be done.
But we really need to accelerate the growth of wind, solar and batteries and have a closer look at that demand growth.
All right.
Professor Brino Gallicor, Director of the Murray Institute and Associate Vice President of Sustainability at UCC.
Thank you for speaking with us this morning.
